newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels braces for rally as demonstrations abound.
newsitem.headline: Brussels braces for rally as demonstrations abound.

text.p: King Albert called for profound change and tens of thousands of people took to the streets across Belgium on Friday for the fourth straight day in a rising tide of demands for a complete clean out of the justice system.

In some places there were minor clashes between protestors and police, and in others traffic was halted by processions of demonstrators outraged at the bungling and incompetence revealed in the country's child abduction, sex and murder scandal.
As Brussels braced for what one newspaper dubbed the March of the Century on Sunday in support of the parents of dead and missing children, a top minister warned the government could go.

"If the government does not listen to the public and does not make sure that the investigation can continue perfectly it could fall over the Dutroux case," Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte told Nieuwe Panorama magazine.

Belgium has been in shock since mid-August when two young sexually-abused girls were rescued from a secret dungeon in a house owned by rapist Marc Dutroux, followed by the discovery of the dead bodies of four others missing for over a year.

"The Queen and I are convinced that this tragedy must be the occasion for a moral rebirth and a profound change in our country," Albert told a round table conference of the parents of missing children.

But the removal from the case on Monday of investigating magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte who had become something of a national hero for his handling of the case, sparked a bushfire of spontaneous demonstrations and speculation of a cover-up.

Connerotte, whose job as an investigating magistrate is to build a balanced file both for and against prosecution, was ordered off the case because he attended a free spaghetti dinner given by a group helping the parents of missing children.
Public disgust has bridged the country's linguistic divide.
On Friday office and factory workers and students with dried spaghetti their hair, demonstrated outside Antwerp's Justice Palace with placards proclaiming "I am ashamed to be a Belgian."
In front of the Justice Palace in Ghent some of the 3,000 students hurdled rocks, bottles and cans at police.
In Brussels about 50 buses carrying symbolic white ribbons and pictures of Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo -- two of the girls found dead in August -- formed a convoy through the city.
One had a broom sticking out of the window reflecting the public demand for a sweep out of corruption.
Earlier some 50 garbage trucks paraded in front of the justice ministry in Brussels
So far 13 people have been charged in connection with the enquiries, and a team of more than 350 police are on the case and still searching for at least seven other missing children.
Sunday's rally, at which police unofficially expect upwards of 100,000 people from all over Belgium and abroad, is being organised by the parents of some of the children.
Weekend leave has been cancelled and 400 police and 1,000 gendarmes will be on duty hoping for an uneventful rally but prepared to stamp out any incidents that may occur.
"We would like to see the march going on in calm and with dignity. That is the way to respect the victims," Deputy Brussels Mayor Freddy Thielemans said on Thursday.
Many of the marchers will be dressed in white and carrying white flowers as a gesture of sympathy.
Belgian railways has already pre-sold 20,000 cut-price tickets and is putting on extra trains, and all the buses in the provinces of Flanders and Liege have been booked for Sunday.
